Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it. Moonshot tells Kimi AI to code away, but leave the hacking alone
Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model […] Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model with around 3 trillion parameters. Unlike conventional AI services that operate entirely through a provider’s servers, open-weight models allow developers to download the underlying model files, run them on their own systems, and modify how they work. Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the model’s training dataset and reinforcement-learning environments to reduce its ability to conduct offensive cyber operations, while retaining its general coding capabilities. The company plans to release the model’s weights on November 4, opening it up to a wider developer community. Moonshot’s internal testing suggests the safeguards have made a measurable difference. Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 81% on the company’s cybersecurity benchmark, which involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. A similar version without the risk-reduction measures scored 90.5%. That represents a 9.5-percentage-point drop in the reported score. However, the results have not been independently verified, and the model reportedly still outperformed its predecessor. The distinction matters because the same AI capabilities can be used for both defence and offence. Security teams could use AI to identify weaknesses in software before criminals exploit them. Attackers, meanwhile, could use models that write code, operate software tools and complete multi-step tasks to automate parts of an attack. Moonshot argues that open-weight AI can help organisations inspect and secure neglected or older software. But once model files are distributed widely, the original developer has less control over who uses them and whether safeguards remain effective. Moonshot’s decision comes as governments and technology companies worry that increasingly capable AI could make sophisticated cyberattacks cheaper and easier to execute. China has also proposed export controls targeting AI-driven malware-generation technology and certain AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The proposals remain subject to public comment. For businesses and ordinary users, the stakes extend beyond individual computers. More automated attacks could increase pressure on organisations responsible for protecting personal information, financial systems and critical infrastructure. At the same time, restricting AI security research too aggressively could leave vulnerabilities undiscovered. Kimi K3.1 Pro also features a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in one go. Moonshot has introduced a Highspeed version that it says runs two to three times faster than the standard model. The next major test will come when Moonshot releases the model weights on November 4. Developers and security researchers will then have greater access to examine its capabilities, while the industry will face a difficult question: can safeguards remain effective once a powerful AI model is available for independent use?

Designing an AI serving harness built to last
The engineering system surrounding an AI model increasingly determines whether its intelligence can be delivered reliably, economically, and at scale. The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures. The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture. That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic. A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't. The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost. Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency. Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance. GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive. The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat. Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements. For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value. Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances. That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy. Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset. EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable. Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes. The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale. This content was produced by EXL. Hackers find a way to turn users' own AI agents and Downloads folders against them
Beware: Your Downloads folder could hold instructions for your AI assistant that you definitely didn’t write. Your Downloads folder probably contains a few PDFs, forgotten screenshots, and several files named some variation of "final." But according to a recent report by security company Forever, it could also contain instructions telling your AI assistant to install malware . In an Oct. 22 blog post , the company reported that they caught an AI coding assistant following those instructions on a customer's computer. The company blocked the installation, then traced the request to a text file in Downloads. How does a text file get that kind of power? Tools like OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code can, depending on their permissions, edit files, run commands, and install software. Developers leave them instruction files called AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md to explain how to work on a project. If you're building a website, those notes might tell the assistant which fonts to use or what to test before finishing. An attacker can leave instructions, too. In this case, the file told the assistant to install "function-color," a software package linked to the MALFEX malware campaign documented by Checkmarx . Forever didn’t establish how the file reached the customer's computer, but its researchers demonstrated one possible route. Depending on browser settings, a website can drop a file into Downloads without asking for approval. If someone then launches their coding assistant in that folder, it could read the file and follow its orders. When Forever tested the customer's file on an isolated computer, it said Codex downloaded and ran the malware. It also changed settings that could make the attacker’s software load in later sessions. "Once it is written, every Codex session on the machine loads the attacker’s server at startup — in any folder, any project," the researchers wrote. "You can leave the folder. The poison stays." The team separately devised a test targeting Claude Code. The attack worked about half the time, redirecting Claude's traffic to a server the researchers controlled. That exposed a login token and allowed them to send commands back for the assistant to execute, illustrating the risk of giving an assistant access to your computer when it can mistake a stranger's instructions for its own assignment. Researchers have pulled off similar tricks before, showing what AI can really do in the wrong hands. In March 2025, Pillar Security researchers got AI coding assistants to slip harmful code into a project by hiding malicious instructions in their coding rules. In April 2026, NVIDIA’s researchers used a poisoned AGENTS.md file to get Codex to sabotage software and conceal the change. This time, though, Forever says it caught an actual attacker trying the trick on a customer's computer. Yikes. Forever recommends keeping coding assistants out of your Downloads folder and checking unfamiliar AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files before letting an agent work in a project. Keep sandboxes enabled to restrict what the assistant can access, and leave approval requirements on so the agent has to ask permission before taking certain actions. If you suspect an assistant has already followed malicious instructions, check its settings for unfamiliar servers or connections and revoke and replace potentially exposed login tokens. Deleting the original text file may not undo changes the assistant has already made. "The thing to watch is not this file or this folder," the researchers wrote. "It is the agent itself — software that reads untrusted input, holds your credentials, and acts with your authority, sitting in a blind spot the old tools were never built to see." PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues
Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company’s recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or […] The post PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues appeared first on Last Word On Gaming. Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company's recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite. Teams can contain up to five humans alongside an unlimited number of AI agents, with $65,000 in cash prizes and development grants worth as much as $50,000 available. Epic promoted the event with the line "Vibe your way to 50K," alongside a Matrix-inspired image contrasting AI-powered developers who can supposedly "ship awesome games in a weekend" with those who "wait months to prototype." The hand offering the proverbial AI red pill has six fingers, in what is either a bad joke or Epic openly trolling people. It's likely the latter, given the response. Epic's official AI MegaJam announcement encourages entrants to bring AI into anything from coding and asset generation to writing and audio. The event can be entered online or in person at Digital Jungle in San Francisco, where teams from companies including Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Meshy, and SpaceXSI are expected to participate. Main-category winners receive up to $7,500, while additional awards include $2,500 for the best solo project, visuals and developer log. There's even a dedicated category for UEFN projects using LLM-powered NPC conversations. Standout projects can then receive continuation grants of up to $50,000. Interestingly, AI is no longer technically mandatory. Epic's original FAQ said participants had to use AI before the company clarified that this was a mistake. The current rules now explicitly answer "Do I have to use AI?" with "No," although describing an event as an "AI MegaJam" while bringing zero AI is presumably one way to make the judges remember you. The reaction has focused particularly heavily on Epic's suggestion that AI lets developers produce in a weekend what traditionally takes months. As one widely shared response noted, game jams have been doing exactly that for decades. "So do y'all think you invented the concept of a game jam or what?" one developer asked, pointing out that Ludum Dare was running 24-hour jams back in 2002. That criticism directly targets the event's marketing. Rapid prototyping isn't a new benefit invented by generative AI; it's effectively the entire reason game jams exist. GamesRadar was even less charitable , describing the event as Epic offering money to "vibe code an AI slop game" while questioning whether the jam can actually demonstrate something traditional developers haven't already been doing for years. The backlash also comes after months of increasingly heated debate around AI game development. Recent experiments have seen Claude used to recreate Terraria overnight , demonstrating both how rapidly AI coding agents are improving and why developers remain concerned about where those capabilities are heading. The MegaJam isn't an isolated experiment. Earlier this month, CEO Tim Sweeney confirmed that Epic is undergoing a "huge pivot" toward AI, moving developers around to pursue what he called "maximum AI acceleration." As such, Epic subsequently described its redesigned launcher as "vibe coded," while Sweeney has repeatedly argued that AI will become a routine part of modern development. Epic isn't alone, either. Capcom has publicly discussed evolving its technology toward an AI-oriented version of the RE Engine , although it has emphasized keeping human creativity at the center of development. Epic's AI MegaJam almost feels less like an experiment and more like a public demonstration of where Tim Sweeney believes game development is heading. The company is offering serious money, unlimited AI agents, and direct access to some of the biggest names in generative AI. The problem is that telling game developers AI means they can finally build something in a weekend is like explaining Super Mario Bros. to Nintendo; they already know how it works and it's an insult to believe they don't. Whether the MegaJam produces genuinely impressive games could therefore matter far more than the marketing. Epic clearly wants AI-assisted development taken seriously, and in November developers will get four days to show whether that confidence is justified.

The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down . Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts. Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer. The first AI swarm testing plan was a simple collaborative one. During this test phase, the researchers tasked 50 agents with building a thriving civilization in three hours. It seems to have tested 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents here, but not any Claude agents . Probably the most interesting insight from this ‘Civ50’ test was that the 50-strong colony never really thrived. After the first night saw zombies take out a large number of agents (but with little penalty) it was noted that “many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.” From then on, the colonists cautiously survived, and there was a tendency toward bureaucracy. As an example, “four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block.” The researchers say this AI agent swarm behavior “felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents.” Next up, the researchers decided to put AI agent swarms into conflict. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added. Those updates will not reach copies already downloaded. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told CSO that the model ships with safeguards built into its weights, but later changes will go elsewhere. “Subsequent safeguard updates are applied to our managed API and future model releases, rather than automatically updating downloaded checkpoints,” Stock said. Asked which attack stages the model had meaningfully helped with in preview traffic, Stock did not name any. He said the most significant gains were in defensive work such as identifying, reproducing and remediating software vulnerabilities. “While our public-preview monitoring showed the model refusing attacks against live targets, we recognise the potential for misuse as capabilities advance and are continuously strengthening our safeguards,” he said. Hugging Face, which hosts the weights, noted in its own launch post that open weights put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. In July, the UK’s AI Security Institute reported that leading open-weight models trailed the closed frontier on cyber tasks by four to seven months. For highly cyber-capable models, open release creates “a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse,” the institute said. Attackers are already putting open-source AI tooling to work. Earlier this month, Microsoft said a China-aligned group used the agentic AI framework ARTEX to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Mistral says the released model can tell defensive work from malicious requests. According to the company, Large 4 refused 96.6% of malicious prompts in the cyber-related portions of the JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and AgentHarm benchmarks, the highest rate it has measured among open models. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said security leaders should read that number narrowly. “Mistral’s 96.6% figure tells you what their model does in their test scenario, not how it will behave with your data, your adversarial use cases, or in production in your environment against motivated attackers,” she said. Mistral is handling a specialized cybersecurity variant differently. Design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense are getting preview access to a version optimized for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming, the company said. Access is “subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards,” the post said, and is limited to systems partners’ own or are authorized to test. The company said the model scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures how well a model finds, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities. The chart in Mistral’s post shows two open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, scoring higher. Mistral also calls Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding, citing leading scores on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.0. Mistral also intends to share relevant adversarial testing findings “while safeguarding sensitive security information,” he said. He did not give a publication date. Under the EU AI Act, models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs) are presumed to carry systemic risk, according to the European Commission . Their providers must assess and mitigate those risks, report serious incidents and maintain cybersecurity protections. Mistral’s post does not say whether Large 4 falls into that category or what risk assessment preceded the release. Stock said Mistral is a full signatory of the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, including its safety and security chapter, which the Commission accepts as one way to demonstrate compliance. He did not say whether Large 4 has been classified as a systemic-risk model. Businesses running a model-as-a-service offering need a separate license. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December. “Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.” Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said. Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.” Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said. “Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added. Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.” Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification. French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month . The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems. Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.” The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes. Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3. The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site. “Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.” The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API. Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves. “Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet." "We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant." Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%. Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. "I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research . Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.
